SPOILER: TEE-Shielded DNN Partitioning of On-Device Secure Inference with Poison Learning

Donghwa Kang Affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), Republic of Korea    Hojun Choe Affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), Republic of Korea    Doohyun Kim Affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), Republic of Korea    Hyeongboo Baek Affiliation: University of Seoul, Republic of Korea    Brent ByungHoon Kang Affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), Republic of Korea
Abstract

Deploying deep neural networks (DNNs) on edge devices exposes valuable intellectual property to model-stealing attacks. While TEE-shielded DNN partitioning (TSDP) mitigates this by isolating sensitive computations, existing paradigms fail to simultaneously satisfy privacy and efficiency. The training-before-partition paradigm suffers from intrinsic privacy leakage, whereas the partition-before-training paradigm incurs severe latency due to structural dependencies that hinder parallel execution. To overcome these limitations, we propose SPOILER, a novel search-before-training framework that fundamentally decouples the TEE sub-network from the backbone via hardware-aware neural architecture search (NAS). SPOILER identifies a lightweight TEE architecture strictly optimized for hardware constraints, maximizing parallel efficiency. Furthermore, we introduce self-poisoning learning to enforce logical isolation, rendering the exposed backbone functionally incoherent without the TEE component. Extensive experiments on CNNs and Transformers demonstrate that SPOILER achieves state-of-the-art trade-offs between security, latency, and accuracy.

Keywords: 
Model privacy On-Device Inference Trusted execution environment

1 Introduction

The proliferation of deep neural networks (DNNs) has made on-device AI—from smartphone face recognition to autonomous delivery—ubiquitous [19]. Processing inference at the edge offers critical benefits: reduced latency, bandwidth conservation, and data privacy. However, this decentralized architecture exposes models to “white-box” environments where physical access is assumed. Unlike cloud-based black-box models, on-device models are vulnerable to model stealing (MS) attacks, where adversaries clone the model’s functionality, compromising the provider’s intellectual property (IP) [38, 27, 16].

To mitigate these threats, trusted execution environments (TEEs) [1, 5] have been adopted to shield model weights. However, executing the entire model within a TEE incurs prohibitive latency overheads (up to 50×50\times) compared to GPU-accelerated execution [37, 24]. To enable practical TEE-based secure inference, a framework must satisfy four imperative requirements: (i) Security: preventing adversaries from replicating the private model’s functionality using components exposed in the rich execution environments (REE); (ii) Efficiency: minimizing latency while maintaining accuracy comparable to REE-only execution; (iii) Feasibility: operating within the strict hardware constraints of commodity TEEs (e.g., secure memory capacity); and (iv) Generality: ensuring applicability across diverse architectures (e.g., CNNs, Transformers) without model-specific dependencies.

Existing TEE-shielded DNN partitioning (TSDP) paradigms fail to simultaneously satisfy these goals. The training-before-partition (TBP) paradigm (Figure 1(a)) splits a pre-trained model but fails security, as the REE-offloaded layers retain residual private information; remedying this via heavy obfuscation [37, 22] violates efficiency. Conversely, the partition-before-training (PBT) paradigm (Figure 1(b)) advances security by isolating TEE components pre-training, yet it remains critically flawed by an inherent structural dependency. Even when employing sophisticated compression techniques like knowledge transfer, these methods typically construct the TEE sub-network by mimicking the backbone’s topology (e.g., distilling GPU-optimized blocks into CPU-bound TEEs). This inescapable architecture-hardware mismatch dictates inefficient execution flows—such as bidirectional slicing [41] or lock-step dual branches [23]—which cause severe synchronization bottlenecks and GPU idling. Ultimately, PBT’s inability to break free from the backbone’s structural legacy imposes a hard ceiling on efficiency, necessitating a paradigm shift.

To transcend these limitations, we propose SPOILER, which exploits a new paradigm: search-before-training (SBT) (Figure 1(c)). Unlike prior approaches bound by the fixed topology of the backbone, SPOILER fundamentally decouples the TEE sub-network using hardware-aware neural architecture search (NAS) [43, 4]. This allows us to discover extremely lightweight, hardware-optimized layers that drastically reduce latency. However, the limited capacity of such compact sub-networks poses a challenge to maintaining high accuracy, necessitating collaborative training with the REE backbone. While this collaboration typically risks exposing private features, we resolve this dilemma via self-poisoning learning. This mechanism creates a symbiotic synergy: NAS achieves extreme efficiency, while poisoning ensures that the requisite collaborative training reinforces logical isolation, rendering the REE backbone functionally incoherent to adversaries without the TEE component.

  • •

    We identify the fundamental limitations of existing partitioning paradigms, specifically the structural dependency and hardware agnosticism of PBT methods.

  • •

    We propose the SBT paradigm and the SPOILER framework, utilizing multi-objective NAS to discover TEE-shielded architectures optimized for specific hardware constraints.

  • •

    We introduce a self-poisoning learning strategy that neutralizes model stealing attacks by rendering the exposed REE components functionally incoherent.

  • •

    Extensive evaluations demonstrate that SPOILER achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) trade-offs between latency, accuracy, and security compared to existing TSDP solutions.

2 Preliminaries and Threat Model

TEE.

TEE is a hardware-isolated enclave designed to guarantee the confidentiality and integrity of code and data [30, 5]. Operating independently from REE, it communicates solely via secure monitor calls (SMC) [2], ensuring that sensitive assets remain protected from privileged REE adversaries [28]. ARM TrustZone [1] is a representative TEE implementation widely deployed in commodity edge devices.

Defender.

We assume the defender is a model provider aiming to protect the private model’s functionality from unauthorized access [27, 16]. Our objective is to mitigate white-box attacks on deployed models, effectively downgrading the threat level to a black-box setting where the TEE exposes only final prediction labels. We assume the victim model utilizes a public pre-trained backbone to enhance accuracy. The private model is securely provisioned to the user device, after which the TEE selectively offloads non-sensitive computations to the REE (GPU) [24, 34]. Consistent with prior works [23, 8], we exclude user input privacy and physical side-channel attacks from our scope.

Attacker and attack scenario.

As illustrated in Figure 2, we consider an adversary with root privileges in the REE who employs a two-step pipeline for MS [15, 38]. First, in model initialization (Step 1), the adversary constructs a shadow model by combining a public model (sharing the victim’s backbone architecture) with the weights exposed in the REE. Next, in model stealing (Step 2), the adversary trains a surrogate model via knowledge distillation, querying the victim model with an auxiliary dataset to generate input-prediction pairs for fine-tuning.

3 Motivation and Design Principles

Figure 3 categorizes existing TSDP approaches into paradigms based on their defense strategies. While executing the entire model within the TEE (❶) theoretically guarantees perfect security, it incurs prohibitive latency due to the lack of GPU acceleration, fundamentally violating efficiency [37, 24]. Consequently, partitioning-based approaches have emerged, yet they face critical trade-offs.

Limitations of TBP: security vs. efficiency.

TBP paradigm splits a pre-trained model. Methods that isolate specific layers (❷) [24, 8] or weights (❸) [13] suffer from intrinsic leakage (violation of security). As shown in Figure 4(a), training the model to retain semantic features (blue line) increases the surrogate model’s accuracy as more of the model is exposed to the REE. In contrast, adversarial training or random (red or green line), which lacks semantic features, degrades the surrogate model’s accuracy even below that of a pretrained model. To mitigate this, approaches like GroupCover [40] (or similar obfuscation methods [37]) (❹) employ heavy obfuscation. However, our measurements on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin [25] reveal that the cryptographic overhead often outweighs data transmission costs (Figure 4(b)), severely compromising efficiency. P1: To ensure security and efficiency, the REE must not contain any private layers capable of learning semantic features, thereby eliminating the need for costly obfuscation.

Limitations of PBT: sequential dependency.

PBT paradigm isolates TEE components pre-training to avoid leakage. Methods like TEESlice [41] (❺) and TBNet [23] (❻) adopt this approach but fail to maximize efficiency. ❺ suffers from high synchronization overheads due to frequent TEE-REE communication [34]. Similarly, ❻ employs a one-way structure but creates a strong sequential dependency where the REE GPU remains idle while waiting for TEE CPU computations. P2: To ensure efficiency, TEE-to-REE data transfer must be minimized, and TEE and REE computations must be decoupled to enable parallel execution.

Lack of feasibility and generality.

Furthermore, all aforementioned methods (❶–❻) rely on static, heuristic-based partitioning. They optimize for theoretical metrics (e.g., FLOPs) rather than real-world latency under varying hardware constraints (e.g., memory limits, power modes), violating feasibility. Additionally, they are often tailored to specific architectures (e.g., CNNs with BatchNorm), lacking generality [23]. To satisfy these principles, our proposed SPOILER (❼) introduces the SBT paradigm. P3: To ensure feasibility and generality, the partitioning strategy must be automatically optimized via hardware-aware search to adapt to diverse model architectures and device constraints.

4 Methodology

In this section, we introduce SPOILER, a novel realization of the SBT paradigm based on P1–P3. SPOILER operates in two phases: (1) hardware-aware architecture search, which identifies the optimal TEE sub-network configuration balancing accuracy and latency (Section 4.1–4.4); and (2) self-poisoning training, which fine-tunes the model to enforce logical isolation, ensuring security without heavy obfuscation (Section 4.5).

4.1 Problem Definition

The primary objective of SPOILER is to discover a TEE sub-network configuration a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} that maximizes accuracy while strictly satisfying hardware constraints. Formally, we define the bi-objective optimization problem as:

maxa∈𝒜\displaystyle\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}} (f⁡(a,W∗​(a)),−g⁡(a))\displaystyle\left(f(a,W^{*}(a)),-g(a)\right) (1)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} W∗​(a)=argminW​ℒt​r​a​i​n​(a,W),ℋ⁡(a)≤ℋl​i​m​i​t\displaystyle W^{*}(a)=\text{argmin}_{W}\mathcal{L}_{train}(a,W),\;\;\mathcal{H}(a)\leq\mathcal{H}_{limit}

where f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) denotes validation accuracy and g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot) represents parallel inference latency (defined in Section 4.2). W∗​(a)W^{*}(a) refers to the optimal parameters trained via the loss function ℒt​r​a​i​n\mathcal{L}_{train} (e.g., cross-entropy). ℋ⁡(a)\mathcal{H}(a) encapsulates the hardware resource usage of configuration aa, which must remain below the hardware constraint threshold ℋl​i​m​i​t\mathcal{H}_{limit} (e.g., available secure memory capacity).

To select the final optimal configuration a∗a^{*} from the Pareto frontier 𝒜∗\mathcal{A}^{*}, we employ a weighted scoring function:

S⁡(a)=α⋅f~​(a)+(1−α)⋅(1−g~​(a)),S(a)=\alpha\cdot\tilde{f}(a)+(1-\alpha)\cdot(1-\tilde{g}(a)), (2)

where f~\tilde{f} and g~\tilde{g} are Min-Max normalized accuracy and latency, and α\alpha balances the trade-off.

4.2 Design of SPOILER

Design principles.

To adhere to P1, the TEE sub-network is designed as an isolated "side-branch" containing semantic features, ensuring no sensitive parameters reside in the REE. This decoupling naturally satisfies P2 by enabling parallel execution between the REE backbone (GPU) and the TEE sub-network (CPU). By enforcing strictly unidirectional data transfer from the REE to the TEE, SPOILER eliminates complex synchronization and obfuscation, maximizing parallel efficiency. To further address P2, SPOILER minimizes data transfer volume using parameter-free adapters. Crucially, to maintain P1 compliance, these adapters compress intermediate features via interpolation without introducing learnable parameters in the REE.

Parallel execution.

The sub-network can comprise up to the same number of blocks as the backbone (e.g., 12 encoders for ViTs, or pooling stages for CNNs), excluding the final classifier. Data transmission to the sub-network initiates only after the input passes at least one backbone block, ensuring every transfer is followed by a sub-network block inference. Let KK and LL denote the number of unidirectional data transfer points and total backbone blocks (excluding the classifier), respectively. Let pkp_{k} be the backbone block index for the kk-th data transfer. The total parallel inference latency for configuration aa is formulated as:

g⁡(a)=∑l=1p1clG+cp1A+∑k=1K−1max⁡(cT​(ak)+cC​(ak),∑l=pk+1pk+1clG+cpk+1A)+max⁡(cT​(aK)+cC​(aK),∑l=pK+1LclG),(K>0),g(a)=\sum_{l=1}^{p_{1}}c^{G}_{l}+c^{A}_{p_{1}}+\sum_{k=1}^{K-1}\max\left(c^{T}(a_{k})+c^{C}(a_{k}),\sum_{l=p_{k}+1}^{p_{k+1}}c^{G}_{l}+c^{A}_{p_{k+1}}\right)\\ +\max\left(c^{T}(a_{K})+c^{C}(a_{K}),\sum_{l=p_{K}+1}^{L}c^{G}_{l}\right),(K>0), (3)

where ciGc^{G}_{i} and cC​(ak)c^{C}(a_{k}) denote the execution times of the ii-th backbone block (GPU) and the kk-th sub-network block with configuration aka_{k} (CPU), respectively. Additionally, ciAc^{A}_{i} and cT​(ak)c^{T}(a_{k}) represent the adapter execution time for data compression and the REE-to-TEE data transmission time.

SPOILER employs a handshake-based parallel execution mechanism; latency per synchronization interval is dictated by the maximum execution time between the backbone and sub-network. The total latency g⁡(a)g(a) is inherently lower-bounded by the pure backbone execution time, ∑l=1LclG\sum_{l=1}^{L}c^{G}_{l}, ensuring the architecture search does not sacrifice accuracy solely for latency optimization. If K=0K=0, SPOILER operates without the sub-network, resulting in g⁡(a)=∑l=1LclGg(a)=\sum_{l=1}^{L}c^{G}_{l}.

4.3 TEE-aware Search Space

Block configuration.

For P3, we construct a unified search space accommodating diverse backbone architectures, including CNNs and Transformers. Inspired by lightweight architectures [14, 36], SPOILER supports both spatial and channel mixing blocks. As depicted in Figure 5, this encompasses token and channel mixing for Transformers, alongside depth-wise and point-wise convolutions for CNNs, enabling the sub-network to optimally balance accuracy and latency.

To minimize latency within the resource-constrained TEE, SPOILER encapsulates these mixing blocks within a bottleneck structure. Specifically, it employs average pooling for down-projection and a linear layer (WuW^{u}) for up-sampling. The bottleneck reduces spatial dimensions (e.g., tokens or resolution) for spatial mixing blocks, and down-samples/up-samples channel dimensions for channel mixing blocks. This design guarantees execution feasibility while preserving representational capacity. Detailed configurations are provided in Section A of the supplementary material.

Search factors.

To systematically formulate the architecture search for the TEE sub-network, we define the configuration a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}. Specifically, the configuration aa is uniquely determined by two global up-sampling factors (Su,CuS^{u},C^{u}) and five block-specific factors (Tk,Skh,Ckh,Skd,CkdT_{k},S^{h}_{k},C^{h}_{k},S^{d}_{k},C^{d}_{k}) for the kk-th sub-network block. First, SuS^{u} and CuC^{u} represent the global spatial and channel up-sampling dimensions, respectively. These are maintained as constant values across all blocks to ensure dimensional compatibility when aggregating the outputs of the sub-network blocks. TkT_{k} denotes the operation type of the kk-th block. For instance, Tk=0T_{k}=0 indicates an inactive block, whereas Tk=1T_{k}=1 and Tk=2T_{k}=2 represent active spatial mixing and channel mixing blocks, respectively. When the kk-th block is active, SkdS^{d}_{k} and CkdC^{d}_{k} define its down-projection dimensions for the bottleneck structure, while SkhS^{h}_{k} and CkhC^{h}_{k} denote its internal hidden dimensions. The detailed value ranges for each search factor are provided in Section A of the supplementary material.

4.4 TEE-aware Neural Architecture Search

Even with constrained search factors, exploring the entire search space is computationally prohibitive. For instance, a 13-block Vision Transformer yields over 102010^{20} possible configurations. To navigate this vast space and realize P3 efficiently, SPOILER employs Bayesian Optimization (BO) with Gaussian Processes (GP) [32]. Specifically, we utilize a sparse axis-aligned subspace GP (SAAS-GP) [9] to effectively handle high-dimensional discrete spaces by identifying sparse relevant dimensions. To reduce computational overhead, SPOILER trains multiple candidate sub-networks in parallel by freezing the backbone weights. Furthermore, SPOILER minimizes search cost by evaluating the objective f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) after a single-epoch training on either a subset or the full dataset.

Driven by the NEHVI acquisition function [6], SPOILER iteratively samples candidate batches to update the SAAS-GP surrogate model. Upon completion, SPOILER extracts the Pareto-optimal solutions and returns the optimal configuration a∗a^{*} that maximizes the score S⁡(a)S(a) in Eq. 2. A detailed algorithmic procedure is provided in Section B of the supplementary material.

4.5 Self-Poisoning Learning

After identifying the optimal sub-network a∗a^{*}, we train the combined architecture. Since the TEE’s strict architectural constraints inherently limit a∗a^{*}’s representational capacity and degrade accuracy, we propose a novel self-poisoning learning to overcome this without violating P1. As analyzed in Section 3, adversarially trained weights actively hinder an attacker’s ability to steal sensitive weights. Leveraging this, our joint objective deliberately "poisons" the standalone backbone, forcing the sub-network to learn highly specialized, complementary representations to maximize the combined accuracy:

ℒt​o​t​a​l=β⋅ℒC​E​(Mc​(x),y)+(1−β)⋅ℒK​D​(Mc​(x),Mt​(x))−λ⋅ℒC​E​(Mb​(x),y),\mathcal{L}_{total}=\beta\cdot\mathcal{L}_{CE}(M_{c}(x),y)+(1-\beta)\cdot\mathcal{L}_{KD}(M_{c}(x),M_{t}(x))-\lambda\cdot\mathcal{L}_{CE}(M_{b}(x),y), (4)

where Mb​(x)M_{b}(x), Mc​(x)M_{c}(x), and Mt​(x)M_{t}(x) are the logits from the standalone backbone, the combined model, and a teacher model, respectively. The hyperparameters β\beta and λ\lambda balance the task-specific objectives (ℒC​E\mathcal{L}_{CE} and ℒK​D\mathcal{L}_{KD} [12]) against the adversarial penalty (−ℒC​E-\mathcal{L}_{CE}) applied to the backbone. Finally, SPOILER employs gradient clipping to maintain stability against the diverging gradients of the adversarial term.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

Experimental environment.

Our experiments are conducted on NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs. For real-world latency measurements, we deploy an NVIDIA Jetson Orin [25] configured to the MAXN power mode. It features a 12-core Arm Cortex-A78AE CPU and 48MB of secure memory, utilizing OP-TEE based on Arm TrustZone [1]. Following [33, 24], the TEE sub-network is established using Darknet [29], while the REE backbone is GPU-accelerated via ONNX Runtime [26]. To maximize parallel efficiency, the REE and TEE execute inference asynchronously, exchanging intermediate features exclusively through a shared memory interface.

Models and datasets.

We evaluate the performance of SPOILER on image classification tasks. Specifically, we employ representative CNN architectures (VGG16-BN [31] and ResNet-18 [11]) alongside a Vision Transformer (ViT-Base [7]) to demonstrate the generalizability of our approach across different architectures. These models are evaluated on the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 [17], and TinyImageNet [18] datasets. Following previous works [41], CNNs process inputs at 32×3232\times 32 for CIFAR and 64×6464\times 64 for TinyImageNet, while ViT-Base resizes all images to 224×224224\times 224.

Evaluation metrics.

We evaluate SPOILER to validate four design goals: security, efficiency, and feasibility, generality. As SPOILER inherently demonstrates generality across diverse architectures, we quantitatively assess the remaining three. Security is measured by the surrogate model’s accuracy (lower indicates stronger protection). Efficiency is evaluated via the victim model’s accuracy and end-to-end inference latency. Lastly, feasibility is validated by execution performance under real-world hardware constraints.

Attack configuration.

Following prior TSDP studies [33, 41], we adopt the threat model of Knockoff Nets [27]. Specifically, the attacker initializes a surrogate model using pre-trained weights from public sources, combined with exposed private weights in the victim’s REE. The attacker then queries the victim model using merely 1% of the training data to collect input-output label pairs for surrogate training.

Baseline defense approaches.

To rigorously evaluate SPOILER, we compare its performance against SOTA TSDP methods from both TBP and PBT paradigms. For the TBP paradigm, we evaluate DarkneTZ [24] and Serdab [8] (protecting the last and first three layers (or blocks) in the TEE, respectively), Magnitude [13] (securing the top 1% largest weights), and GroupCover [40] (obfuscating linear layers in the REE while executing non-linear layers in the TEE). For the PBT paradigm, TEESlice [41] secures a sub-network alongside non-linear layers in the TEE, whereas TB-Net [23] protects only the sub-network. 11 1 Since the official implementations for TEESlice (ViT-Base) and TB-Net are not publicly available, we carefully re-implemented these methods based on the details provided in the original papers. Finally, we define two reference scenarios: No-shield (all weights exposed to the REE, enabling direct copying without additional training) and Black-box (no weights leaked, restricting the attacker to pre-trained weights and input-output label queries).

5.2 Results: Security

For the architecture search, we set α=0.5\alpha=0.5 and the TEE memory limit to ℋl​i​m​i​t=24\mathcal{H}_{limit}=24MB. For self-poisoning learning, the adversarial factor λ\lambda is set to 0.01, 0.001, and 0.005 for VGG16-BN, ResNet-18, and ViT-Base, with gradient clipping thresholds of 0.5, 2.0, and 2.0, respectively.

Table 1 compares the attacker’s surrogate model accuracy across defense methods. Most TBP methods fail to prevent model extraction, yielding higher surrogate accuracies than the Black-box baseline, except GroupCover which obfuscates REE weights. Within the PBT paradigm, TEESlice provides Black-box-level defense, while TB-Net further reduces surrogate accuracy. Notably, SPOILER consistently records the lowest surrogate accuracy across most models and datasets. For instance, with ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, SPOILER drastically suppresses surrogate accuracy to 12.36%, outperforming the most secure SOTA baseline (GroupCover, 34.44%). This demonstrates that adversarially spoiling the backbone network effectively neutralizes model stealing attacks.

5.3 Results: Efficiency

Accuracy.

Table 2 compares the classification accuracy of the combined model (the backbone coupled with the sub-network) searched and trained via SPOILER against the fully fine-tuning victim model (No-Shield). SPOILER achieves comparable or even superior accuracy compared to the baseline across most models and datasets. Remarkably, for ResNet-18 on TinyImageNet, SPOILER demonstrates a significant accuracy improvement of approximately 7.4%p (68.68% vs. 61.28%). This highlights that SPOILER does not sacrifice accuracy to enforce strict security; rather, SPOILER often enhances the model’s inherent performance.

Latency.

To demonstrate the efficiency of SPOILER, we average 100 latency measurements on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin. As shown in Figure 6, we compare SPOILER against an unprotected GPU baseline (No-shield) and DarkneTZ (isolating the final 1, 2, and 3 layers). DarkneTZ inherently suffers from the critical flaws shared by all sequential TSDP methods: strict sequential bottlenecks and hardware-oblivious memory allocation. Consequently, isolating just two layers often triggers Out-Of-Memory (OOM) faults, while layer-by-layer weight loading incurs high I/O overheads. Conversely, by leveraging NAS and strictly bounding the secure memory via ℋl​i​m​i​t\mathcal{H}_{limit}, SPOILER easily fits and executes the sub-networks of heavy models like ViT-Base in a single pass. By enabling asynchronous parallel execution, SPOILER significantly outperforms TSDP baselines. Notably, for VGG16-BN on CIFAR-100, SPOILER even surpasses No-shield’s speed, as the independent sub-network can terminate without waiting for the entire backbone inference to finish.

Trade-off between accuracy and latency.

Figure 7 presents the accuracy of sub-network configurations derived across varying values of α\alpha in Eq. (2). As α\alpha increases, the task accuracy remains stable, exhibiting a marginal upward trend. This stability demonstrates the efficacy of SPOILER’s architectural design, indicating that SPOILER consistently isolates high-capacity sub-networks regardless of minor hyperparameter shifts. Crucially, the accuracy benefits identified during the NAS phase are seamlessly preserved in the final models, even after self-poisoning learning. This end-to-end stability allows SPOILER to offer multiple valid configuration candidates from just a single search phase, ensuring high accuracy for diverse user constraints.

5.4 Results: Feasibility

To simulate diverse edge devices, we evaluate SPOILER across four Jetson Orin power modes (15W, 30W, 50W, and MAXN). Figure 8 illustrates the security-accuracy trade-off controlled by the adversarial factor λ\lambda (α,β=0.5\alpha,\beta=0.5). SPOILER utilizes λ\lambda as a flexible control knob between security and accuracy: a higher λ\lambda enforces stricter security against model stealing, whereas a lower λ\lambda prioritizes the primary task accuracy. Notably, the circle markers in the figure highlight the optimal configurations (the ‘sweet spots’) where SPOILER successfully suppresses the surrogate accuracy below the Black-box baseline while restricting the accuracy drop to within a mere 3%p compared to the fully fine-tuned victim model. Crucially, at least one such optimal configuration exists across all tested power modes, datasets, and architectures. This demonstrates that by calibrating λ\lambda, SPOILER seamlessly adapts to various hardware constraints, thoroughly spoiling backbone weights to prevent extraction without sacrificing inherent performance.

6 Related Work

6.1 TEE-Shielded Partitioning

Existing TSDP methods fall into two categories: obfuscation-based and static partitioning. Obfuscation methods (e.g., ShadowNet [34], TransLinkGuard [20]) offload transformed layers to GPUs but incur prohibitive cryptographic overheads during the encryption and decryption phases [40]. Conversely, static partitioning frameworks (e.g., DarkneTZ [24], TBNet [23], TEESlice [41]) isolate sensitive layers within the TEE. However, their reliance on strict sequential dependencies forces highly inefficient lock-step synchronization between the TEE (CPU) and REE (GPU). This architectural rigidity causes severe resource idling and exacerbates frequent communication overhead. To overcome these limitations, SPOILER employs TEE-aware NAS to dynamically decouple the TEE sub-network from rigid backbone constraints.

6.2 NAS for Efficient Inference

Hardware-aware NAS frameworks (e.g., MnasNet [35], ProxylessNAS [4], NetAdapt [39], MCUNet [21]) co-optimize architectures for task utility and device constraints like latency or memory. Recent advances also explore supernet training (OFA [3]) and adversarial robustness (RobNets [10]). Furthermore, paradigms like AutoPEFT [42] have shifted focus toward searching for lightweight sub-modules, such as adapters, rather than optimizing the entire backbone. However, whether targeting full architectures or sub-modules, existing NAS literature predominantly focuses on accuracy or input robustness. They do not explicitly account for model confidentiality and the unique constraints of TEEs, such as stringent secure memory limits and severe cross-domain synchronization overheads. SPOILER bridges this gap by explicitly integrating TEE-specific hardware constraints into the search space, simultaneously optimizing for inference efficiency and logical isolation.

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduce SPOILER, a novel defense framework designed to protect model privacy against model stealing attacks on resource-constrained edge devices. To overcome the limitations of existing TSDP paradigms bound by fixed topologies and costly obfuscation, SPOILER pioneers the SBT paradigm. Specifically, it leverages TEE-aware NAS to decouple lightweight TEE sub-networks for parallel execution. Furthermore, to actively disrupt model extraction while preserving the primary task utility, we propose an adversarial self-poisoning learning. Extensive hardware evaluations confirm SPOILER’s seamless adaptability to stringent constraints, jointly optimizing security, latency, and accuracy.
